comments.author: @robinbrown3347
comments.text: Over 60 years ago I flew along the western shoreline of James and Hudson Bay in a small plane. For hours I saw the changing landscape below me and not a single trace of any civilation. I have never seen anything so desolate. Looking at a map of Canada you haven't even begun to go north. Canada is BIG!

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: That must have been an incredible flight! I can only imagine looking down for hours and seeing almost nothing but wilderness. You're absolutely right about Canada's size. It's hard to appreciate just how vast and remote some of these places are until you've actually been there. Do you remember where your flight started and ended? I'd love to look up that route. Thanks for sharing such a great memory!

comments.author: @stevegarcia3731
comments.text: All this is explained with the Lithoshift-ATL hypothesis, and the numbers here are being misread.  We tied the YDIH with the Late Pleistocene Mass Extinction Event.  And it all fits together.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: Interesting perspective! The Younger Dryas is a much more recent event, while the Shield's formation goes back billions of years. I'm always open to corrections, though. Which specific numbers do you believe were misread? If you share the timestamp and source, I'd be happy to look into it.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: Fair point. The age is what makes the Shield fascinating, but the bigger story is really what’s inside it, iron, nickel, gold, uranium, diamonds, and how difficult it can be to mine, process, and move those resources out of such remote terrain. I touched on that with Sudbury, the Ring of Fire and the railway section, but the transportation side could honestly be a whole video on its own.
